summary: Friends and colleagues of Robin Williams describe his cocaine use in Vice's "The Dark Side of Comedy" documentary series, which premiered its second season with his episode. They recall his heavy drug use in the late 1970s and early 1980s, and how John Belushi's 1982 death and the birth of his first son in 1983 helped him quit. Williams died by suicide on Aug. 11, 2014, and an autopsy later showed he had Lewy body dementia and no illegal drugs or alcohol in his system.
one_line: Friends in Vice's "The Dark Side of Comedy" recall Robin Williams' cocaine addiction, his quitting after Belushi's death, and his later undiagnosed Lewy body dementia.
key_facts: Vice's "The Dark Side of Comedy" documentary series covered Robin Williams' drug use in an episode that premiered the show's second season.
Robin Williams began in stand-up comedy in the 1970s and gained fame as the alien Mork on "Happy Days," which led to the series "Mork and Mindy."
Williams also appeared in the film "Popeye" early in his career.
Gina Hecht, his "Mork and Mindy" co-star, said "Robin's highs were so high and his lows were often low."
Allan Stephan recalled Williams asking for cocaine before a show, saying "I can't go on without the blow"; Stephan refused, and Williams reportedly stopped getting high before performing.
Mike Binder said Williams took a gram of cocaine into a bathroom in the '80s and returned with it empty around 8:15 at night, and said "With drugs, he was a monster."
Howie Mandel said cocaine was a big part of Williams' routine at The Comedy Store, even as audiences laughed.
John Belushi died in 1982 of a drug overdose at the Chateau Marmont hotel in West Hollywood, and his death "threw cold water" on Williams.
Belushi's death and the 1983 birth of Williams' first son helped him clean up, and Stanley Wilson said Williams quit cocaine "cold turkey."
After quitting, Williams' career grew, with roles in "Mrs. Doubtfire," "Good Will Hunting" and "Night at the Museum."
Williams died by suicide on Aug. 11, 2014, and was diagnosed posthumously with Lewy body dementia after an autopsy.
Lewy body dementia is the second most common type of dementia after Alzheimer's, according to the Mayo Clinic.
The autopsy found no illegal drugs or traces of alcohol in Williams' system.
Comedian Steven Pearl said Williams was thin, hardly spoke and did not recognize Pearl's wife the last time he saw him.
